A later `MoveNext()` returns `false`; the consumer's eventual `Dispose()` finds nothing pending. Async frames fault their task and tear down at that terminal state. No escape.

The v0.333 form-(iv) face (a static slot moved inside a window an exception crosses) is gone with the form (K9.4 bars any `move` of static storage). Static initialization failure is C4's; a throwing static disposer is C12's.

An `owned` constructor argument is the callee's from call entry: undischarged, the constructor's exception-path discharge disposes it (several of them now in a stated reverse declaration order, #5747); once stored, §22.9's owned-field unwind does; captured, the capture moved it. Re-hunted at v0.334: `new Holder(x, move x)` is now rejected at the `move` (#5750 ruling, a live borrow at the consume), and an uncaptured primary parameter is named in §28.3's order sentence. Unbound temporaries join the same stack at their production."

A `using var` (and the compiler-introduced slots) in a constructor body is disposed on the construction-unwind edge as on every exit edge; §28.10's new parenthetical (process termination unwinds nothing, #5779) is not a construction edge. The only thing the text lets leak is a raw resource held in no owned field, §28.4's recorded one-resource-per-wrapper discipline (no K1 obligation). No escape.

cells.rule: §28.3: "When the full expression is instead exited by an **exception** — an operand or argument evaluated later throws before the temporary's transfer or consumption point — every already-produced, not-yet-consumed unbound owned temporary is disposed during unwinding" | §28.8.1: "where the raise happens **before** the call is entered — a later argument's evaluation throwing — the already-produced temporary has not transferred and is disposed by the caller's unwinding pass." | K8: "Unbound owned temporaries are disposed at their full expression's end, after their uses, in reverse production order — on the normal edge as on the exception edge, where the pass runs during unwinding."

Temporaries produced in a `new` argument list, a field initializer or a constructor body are unwound in reverse production order; one already transferred into an `owned` constructor parameter is the callee's. Side note kept for L1/C1: K8's enumerated full-expression positions still do not name a constructor's chaining-position arguments (`base(...)`, `this(...)`, the inheritance-clause call); the unwind edge is unaffected.

cells.cite: §22.8, §22.9, §22.10, §28.2 (The compiler-inserted free), §28.4, §28.8.1 (The window is straight-line; The vacated location), K9.2, K9.3

Re-hunted at v0.334: (1) a constructor body that `move`s a field and then runs a `new` whose constructor throws inside the window leaves the field in the vacated state, which §22.9's unwind (§28.4's cascade) disposes nothing through, while the taken value is an owned local the exception-path discharge disposes: once. (2) A constructor body's explicit `_r.Dispose()` before a throw: the unwind's `Dispose()` now reads a live flag (0162), so it is the no-op in both modes. No escape.

cells.rule: §28.11: "Disposal of the collection itself — at the end of a `using var` scope, in a destructor's auto-dispose pass, or at static-program-exit for a `static owned` field — disposes every element it still holds, then frees the backing storage" | §22.9: "An exception in the **constructor body** (step 3) triggers disposal of every owned field assigned during initialization (step 2) and the base subobject. Owned fields assigned imperatively in the body are also disposed if assigned successfully before the throwing statement." | K3.15: "**Edge parity.** The exception edge performs the same implicit disposal as the normal edge, on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack; the only difference is the lint. Unbound temporaries join the same stack at their production."
cells.cite: §28.11 (Owning collections), §22.9, §28.3 (Unbound owned temporaries), K3.15
cells.note: An owning collection held in an owned field is disposed by §22.9's unwind and cascades over its elements; one held in a constructor local or temporary is disposed by the exception-path discharge. Elements produced for a literal or an `Add` whose evaluation is cut short by a throw are unbound temporaries (disposed by the unwind) until they are taken by the collection, after which the collection's cascade owns them. No escape found. Re-checked at v0.334: `Clear()` is now a named multi-value pass; nothing on this path moved.

cells.note: Closed by the #5789 ruling (reading B). §28.4 step 2 now names every field of move-only value type, owning-choice fields included (nullable or not, concretely and at a move-only substitution of a bare-`T` field), and §15.3 names §22.9's unwind among the lists, so the v0.333 counterexample's `Res` is disposed on both the unwind and the normal teardown. Owning-inline-array fields unchanged (slots reverse, null-guarded). Re-hunted: an owning-choice field not yet assigned at the throw (assigned-before-the-throwing-statement tracking, §22.9), and a generic `Box<T>` field at an owning-choice substitution (per instantiation). #5799 (whether `owned` may mark such a field) does not move a disposal verdict.

cells.rule: §31.1: "ownership transfers to the runtime's exception machinery, which disposes the exception after the matching catch arm completes" | §22.9: "a disposer that throws during it **supersedes** that exception under [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s rule, and the superseded exception is recorded into the superseding one's `SupersededChain` before the drop" | §22.7: "the original exception never propagates raw out of static initialization; it is observable only as `InnerException`." | §31.4: "**The cached `TypeInitializationException` and its `InnerException` are runtime-owned for the life of the process**" | §30.5: "The task's own block stays live until that terminal state"
cells.cite: §31.1 (Exception ownership), §22.9, §28.4, §31.2, §22.7, §31.4, §30.5 (Disposing an unsettled task), #5788 (closed)
cells.note: Sub-shapes: (1) the in-flight construction exception is the runtime's, disposed once after its catch arm, or superseded during the unwind and then disposed once after its snapshot is recorded: once. (2) A static initializer's escaping exception becomes the cached `TypeInitializationException`'s `InnerException`, and both are runtime-owned for the process and exempt from dispose-after-arm, which is what makes every later re-raise sound: exempt. (3) Supersession of the cached instance drops it undisposed (§31.2). Hunted: re-raising the cached TIE on every touch after a catch arm completed (exempt by name, so no double dispose). No escape. New sub-shape checked at v0.334: an unsettled task held in an owned field of an object whose construction throws is disposed by §22.9's unwind under §30.5's new unsettled-task rule (proposal 0168): the frame's late delivery is disposed by the attached continuation and the task's block stays live until its terminal state. Once.

The call transfers the argument into the frame it mints" | §30.1: "An async method's `owned` parameters transfer into the state-machine frame at call time, exactly as an iterator's do" | §31.4: "Allocation failure is not an exception. There is no `OutOfMemoryException`; nothing is catchable; no unwinding runs"
cells.note: Unchanged. No constructor is a deferred activation; a frame is minted by its call, which runs no user code before its `owned` arguments are frame-held, and its only failure is allocation failure, which unwinds nothing. Proposal 0167's single-consumption iterable changes who disposes the parameters later (C11), not construction.

A static `owned` field on a type left in a failed state ([§22.7](#sec-constructors)) whose initializer *did* complete successfully before the failing initializer is disposed normally." | §22.13: "the pass drains until no initialized-but-undisposed static `owned` field remains" | §22.13: "A static field of owning-inline-array type whose initializer threw is not disposed (the array's slots were never observable)" | §22.13: "A `static readonly` field of class type or interface type that is not marked `owned` is exempt from the [§28.8](#sec-ownership-transfer) ownership-discharge requirement" | §22.7: "The runtime makes no guarantee about ordering of disposal across types when one of the types is in a failed state."

Unchanged otherwise: a field assigned in the static constructor body is enrolled through the drain's 'initialized-but-undisposed' wording, and the cross-type exit order among failed types is explicitly unspecified (order only).

Hunted for an exemption leak: a closure built in a constructor over an owned local (a capture is a borrow, §28.9; a plain function-typed primary parameter cannot be captured into a field, §22.10), and a boxed owning choice (not admitted, §35.8). No obligation-bearing value hides behind the exemption on this path.

cells.rule: §28.3: "A **moved-from** or **explicitly-disposed** LHS is an owned-state LHS holding no live value: it requires an owned RHS and displaces nothing" | §28.2: "the overwrite for a displaced value ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields))" | §28.2: "so the `Dispose()` the language itself issues there — the cascade over an explicitly disposed field, a drop-on-overwrite over an explicitly disposed value, the exit pass — reads a live flag in both modes" | §28.7: "if the previous value is live (non-null and not moved-from" | K3.9: "reclamation at the holder's release point ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s compiler-inserted free)"
cells.cite: §28.3 (State match on reassignment), §28.2 (The compiler-inserted free), §28.7, K1 state 4, K3.9, K3.11, K5.2, K7.4, proposal 0162 §8 item 8 (non-normative), #5768, #5759
cells.note: Ordinary displacement is unchanged and once-backstopped (RHS first, null-guarded drop, K5.2 freeze, K4.1 flag on surviving non-local borrows; §28.7's scope now lists every owned location, #5747). Opened at v0.334 by a composition seam between the #5768 ruling (W4) and proposal 0162 (W3): §28.3 says an explicitly-disposed LHS holds no live value and displaces nothing, and its maybe-consumed sentence disposes 'nothing' on the explicitly-disposed paths. But under 0162 the explicitly disposed block is live until its holder's release point, §28.2 names 'a drop-on-overwrite over an explicitly disposed value' as a language-issued `Dispose()` at a release point, and §28.7's own liveness test (non-null, not moved-from) calls the value live. Reading A (§28.3): the overwrite frees nothing and the binding's later release point frees only the new value, so the disposed block is never reclaimed (a leak of the free obligation; the destructor itself runs once). Reading B (§28.2/§28.7, and 0162's own composition note): the overwrite is the release point (a no-op `Dispose()`, then the free). The same seam reaches a frame-resident local (R8) and a discarded move-only local (R6).

cells.rule: A5: "`using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out" | §28.10: "`using var` is a scope pin (axiom [A5](#sec-axiom-register)): it is implicitly non-reassignable, and reassigning a `using var` variable is a compile error." | §28.3: "establishing a hidden, unnameable `using var` slot"

cells.rule: §28.7: "a throwing disposer during overwrite propagates after the store is abandoned, leaving the new value an unbound owned temporary disposed by [§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)'s unbound-temporary rule — on this exception edge, during the unwind." | §28.3: "A temporary that is instead bound (to a `var`/`using var`), `move`d, returned, or transferred into an owning location is governed by the corresponding transfer or discharge rule and is **not** disposed under this rule (it would otherwise be disposed twice)."

cells.note: An unbound temporary is not a location and cannot be displaced; the one R3 shape on this path is the RHS of an abandoned store (a throwing displaced disposer), which §28.7 makes an unbound owned temporary disposed once by the unwind; the owning-inline-array per-slot pass abandons its store the same way. A binding-atom binding cannot be reassigned inside its single-expression body. No escape found.

cells.rule: §28.7: "The right-hand side is evaluated first; then, if the previous value is live (non-null and not moved-from — the per-slot tracking [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)'s indexer-set rule already defines), it is disposed; then the new value is stored." | §28.8.1: "In checked disposal mode a read of it through any spelling other than this body's tracked one — an alias of the holder, code run inside the window (a constructor body, a destructor, a callee where the window admits calls) — faults as `DisposedAccessException`" | §28.8.1: "a store into it other than the restoring store faults the same way **before** storing" | §28.8.1: "a store into an `owned` field, a plain-`var` owned local, or an owning-collection slot that may hold a live (non-null, not moved-from) value is **throwable**" | §28.7: "a borrow of the displaced value is invalidated at the overwrite, caught as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode and undefined unchecked"

A variant that reaches the vacated field without a throwable form (a `move _r` inside the window, or a constructor body run by a `new`) meets the vacated state, which faults in checked mode before any store, so the restoring store displaces nothing; unchecked, it is K4.1's undefined behavior. Ordinary overwrite, incl. `set(owned)`: once-backstopped as before; an overwrite of an explicitly disposed field reads a live flag (0162).

(2) A slot vacated by `move o._slots[i]` through an alias of the holder is a vacated location: the v0.333 counterexample's `_slots[0] := new Res()` is an inline-array indexer access (throwable) inside the straight-line window, so rejected; any non-throwable reach meets the checked-mode fault. Whole-value reassignment of an inline array (per live slot, reverse) and of an owning choice or `C?` (one value; `:= null` drops): once. A discarded move-only local that is then reassigned inherits R1/C6's explicitly-disposed seam for its slot objects' blocks (L2-RV1); that is filed under R1/C6, not here.

cells.rule: §30.11: "The `Set*` methods complete the task; `TrySet*` returns `false` instead of throwing when the task is already in a terminal state." | §30.11: "If `TrySetResult` returns `false` because the task is already in a terminal state, the implementation disposes `result` before returning." | §28.8.1: "If the call then raises — from the callee's body, or from a constructor's field initializers or body ([§22.9](#sec-owned-fields-and-exception-safety)) — the caller's binding is moved-from on the exception edge exactly as on the normal one, and the value is discharged on the callee's side" | §31.2: "the superseded exception is **disposed by the runtime exactly once**, as if its handling had completed"
cells.note: Runtime-held slots are write-once: a task's result or fault is set at its terminal state and never displaced. A second `Set*` throws, and its `owned` argument is the stdlib method's parameter, discharged on the callee's side by §28.8.1; a failing `TrySet*` disposes its argument. The in-flight exception's 'displacement' is supersession, disposed once after its snapshot is recorded, with the two owner-owned instances dropped undisposed. Static task caches overwritten in place are R9's exemption. v0.334: a task-typed owned field or local overwritten while its task is unsettled takes §30.5's new continuation (proposal 0168): the block stays live until the terminal state and the late delivery is disposed there; once.

cells.rule: §28.12: "The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §28.12: "always take the synchronous `Dispose()` path, on every edge and in every context including `async` bodies" | K5: "the frame's own disposal — explicit, at a `using var`'s scope end, or [K3.14](#sec-kernel-k3)'s auto-drop — counting as a use" | §29.8: "where no enumerator was produced, the iterable disposes the parameter when it is itself disposed"
cells.note: Frame-resident reassignment takes §28.7 synchronously. A displaced frame's disposal runs its pending cleanup and counts as a use for the freeze. New at v0.334 (0167): overwriting a local that holds an iterable minted over an `owned` parameter and never enumerated disposes the parameter with the iterable; an unsettled async task overwritten takes §30.5's continuation (0168). Once-backstopped. An explicitly disposed frame-resident local reassigned is R1/C6's seam (L2-RV1).

cells.note: Closed by form (iv)'s retirement (proposal 0162 item 5). The v0.333 open face, a slot store into a mutable static owning inline array, is now unwritable: a mutable static of that type is rule 2's closing error, and the `static readonly` form's slots are fixed (a slot store is a K9.4 compile error). Sub-shapes: `static owned readonly` and note (h): single assignment, no displacement (rejected/n/a in effect); admitted non-`owned` mutable statics: exempt by the recorded no-drop posture. cells.note: Overwriting a `string`, `Type`, box or function value displaces no obligation. Hunted: a function-typed field whose closure captured an owned local (the capture is a borrow, rejected past its source, §28.9), and an interface-typed owned field holding a box (the drop is §28.9's no-op). Nothing obligation-bearing is displaced silently.

If a later disposal in the same pass also throws, the later exception **supersedes** the earlier one"

Several locals: reverse declaration order, a throwing disposer leaving the rest running with supersession. The return slot (#5781) joins the same stack on a `return` edge. Once.

If a later disposal in the same pass also throws, the later exception **supersedes** the earlier one"

Scope-end disposal of several locals is a named multi-value pass, in which a throwing disposer does not stop the rest and later throws supersede with record-before-drop. A borrow-pin contributes nothing to the pass. No escape found.

Unbound temporaries join the same stack at their production." | K8: "disposed at the atom's completion if undischarged, after the body's evaluation, in reverse clause order"

Binding-atom bindings go in reverse clause order and a `case` scrutinee's temporary lasts the construct. Re-hunted: a chain over a `new` root (#5780) is now a borrow of the unbound temporary, so it adds no second owned temporary to the pass. Once.

Re-hunted at v0.334's new flag moments (0162 item 2): a child's destructor reaching the parent through a back-reference during the field cascade finds the parent already logically disposed (the cascade runs after logical disposal completes), so the K4.1 fault still stands behind it; an alias reaching the parent during its destructor body meets a live instance whose cascade has not run, so any value it stores into an owned field is disposed by that cascade. A cascade over an explicitly disposed field reads a live flag. Once.

cells.note: The cascade order is stated per type (unordered types explicitly implementation-defined), and the v0.333 note is closed: `Clear()` is now a named §28.4 pass that leaves the collection empty when an exception leaves it (#5747). Exactly-once no longer leans on idempotence. Once.

cells.note: Closed by the #5789 ruling. Owning inline arrays: reverse slot order, a multi-value pass, the holder's destruction leaving §9.4's disposed state. Owning choices: payloads in declaration order, now stated as a ruling for the kind (#5747 item 7). At an instance field, §28.4 step 2 and §28.9's trivial-dispose definition both name owning-choice fields, so the class's generated `Dispose()` disposes the choice at its place in reverse declaration order and the class is not trivial-dispose. Once.

cells.rule: §28.4: "a pass entered with **no exception in flight** whose N disposers all throw leaves the escaping exception carrying N−1 chronological entries" | §31.2: "a superseded task-owned fault instance ([§30.9](#sec-exception-handling-in-async-methods)) or cached `TypeInitializationException` ([§31.4](#sec-standard-exception-types)) is dropped from the in-flight slot **undisposed**" | §31.2: "**Self-supersession records nothing:**"
cells.cite: §28.4 (multi-value pass accounting), §31.2 (supersession, record-before-drop, per-raise chain), §22.9, §22.13, §30.9, §31.4
cells.note: Ordinary in-flight and superseded exceptions in a pass: each superseded one is snapshotted into the superseder's `SupersededChain` and then disposed once (once). Task-owned faults and the cached TIE are dropped undisposed and stay with their owner (exempt). Accounting: N−1 entries with no exception in flight, plus the in-flight exception's own entry ahead of them on an exception edge. The exit pass reports rather than propagates. No escape.

cells.rule: §29.7: "in reverse order of establishment, exactly as if the body had exited at the suspension point" | §29.8: "The order across multiple owned parameters is reverse declaration order, mirroring [§28.4](#sec-the-destructor)'s destructor rule." | §30.1: "on every completion path (success, fault, and cancellation), after the body's `using var` cleanups and `finally` clauses, in reverse declaration order"
cells.cite: §29.7, §29.8, §30.1, §28.12 (implicit discharge synchronous), §28.4, K3.15
cells.note: Frame teardown runs pending cleanups in reverse establishment, then undischarged `owned` parameters in reverse declaration order, on every terminal path, a body fault now being a completion (#5765). Under 0167 the enumerator disposes them, or the iterable where no enumerator was produced; either way one pass. Once.

cells.rule: §22.13: "Static `owned` fields are disposed at program exit, after `Main` completes (normally, or by an uncaught exception — [§33.3](#sec-exit-code) defines the exit code for each), in **reverse order of static initialization** across all types" | §22.13: "**What escapes the pass is reported, not propagated.**" | §22.13: "Static `owned` fields initialized during the pass join it" | §22.13: "The field is not disposed at program exit and must not hold resources that require explicit cleanup."
cells.cite: §22.12 rule 1, §22.13 (Disposal of static owned fields; throwing destructor; exemption; abnormal termination), §15.1.1, §28.4, §31.2, §33.3
cells.note: `static owned` fields and note (h)'s `static readonly` owning inline arrays: disposed once by the exit pass in reverse initialization order across types, reverse declaration order within a type, slots in reverse, late initializations drained, throws superseded and reported. Non-`owned` statics: exempt. No explicit early disposal of a static owned field is admitted any longer (0162 item 4), so the pass never meets one. The v0.333 re-population route is n/a (below).

cells.rule: §15.1.1: "A slot of interface type holding a boxed value type ([§8.6](#sec-boxing)) holds a runtime-managed value ([§28.9](#sec-runtime-managed-types)): the pass runs no user code for it, the box's `Dispose()` being §28.9's no-op." | K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation"
cells.note: A runtime-managed value inside a pass (a boxed slot, a string or function field) contributes a no-op step and no supersession. Hunted: a closure held in a field of an object in a pass that captured an owned referent (capture is a borrow; reclaiming the closure never leaves a destructor un-run, §28.9). Nothing obligation-bearing rides the exemption.

cells.rule: K3.3: "an `owned` argument ([§22.3](#sec-parameter-modifiers)) | `move x` at the call site | **moved-from** | frozen (K5.1) | none here — the callee's" | §28.8.1: "The transfer of an `owned` argument completes when the call is **entered**" | K3.13: "An **unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes**" | §28.3: "A borrow of the consumed binding passed as an argument or operand evaluated **before** a consuming argument of the same call ([§22.5](#sec-optional-parameters-and-named-arguments)'s textual order) is such a borrow, its use being the call itself" | §28.3: "`Sink(x, move x)` and `Sink(x.Child(), move x)` are rejected at the `move`" | K5.5: "an argument or operand of the same full expression evaluated before the consume and used by its call or operator"
cells.cite: K3 table (K3.1–K3.4, K3.7), K3.13, K5, K5.5, §22.3, §22.4, §22.5, §28.3 (Move semantics; *The consume-site freeze*), §28.8.1 (raise from the consuming call), App. C.3; #5750 (closed, ruling reading 1), #5811 (impl tracker), #5813 (impl-ahead mirror)
cells.note: Every marked transfer of an owned local or `owned` parameter of a synchronous body leaves it moved-from. The new holder discharges, the scope-end and unwind passes skip the binding, and a raise after entry stays with the callee (§28.8.1). An unmarked read only borrows. `out owned` delivers only on normal return. The v0.333 opening is closed by the #5750 ruling: a borrow of the consumed binding passed as an earlier argument or operand is live at the consume, so `Sink(x, move x)` and `Sink(x.Child(), move x)` are rejected. A value-typed read (`Add(x.Id, move x)`) is unaffected. Hunted and closed: `M(move x, x.F())` (the second operand reads a moved-from binding); a named argument written after the move (`Sink(c: move x, view: x)`; §22.5 textual order makes it a moved-from read); `Sink(x.AsSpan(), move x)` (a span holds borrows of `x`); `x.Absorb(move x)` (the receiver is an operand evaluated before the consume and used by the call, K5.5 clause 5); a closure argument over `x` (a live closure). `new T(move n, n)` is #5813's impl-ahead delta, not a spec gap.

cells.rule: K7.4: "owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path" | K1: "**maybe-consumed** — the K7 join of owned with moved-from or explicitly-disposed; unreadable until reassigned (a reassignment displaces per path and leaves the binding owned" | §28.3: "A **moved-from** or **explicitly-disposed** LHS is an owned-state LHS holding no live value: it requires an owned RHS and displaces nothing ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s liveness test)." | §28.3: "A **maybe-consumed** LHS ([K1](#sec-kernel-k1) state 4) is an owned-state LHS whose displaced value exists on exactly the paths that did not consume it: the store requires an owned RHS, disposes the displaced value on those paths and nothing on the others" | §28.7: "if the previous value is live (non-null and not moved-from — the per-slot tracking [§28.11](#sec-collection-element-ownership)'s indexer-set rule already defines), it is disposed" | §28.2: "Every class instance is reclaimed by compiler-inserted code at its **holder's release point** — scope end for a local, a `using var` or an `owned` parameter" | §28.2: "does not reclaim its receiver: the receiver's block stays live until the holder's release point" | §28.2: "the overwrite for a displaced value" | §28.2: "a drop-on-overwrite over an explicitly disposed value"
cells.cite: K1 (states 3–4, explicitly-disposed), K3.9, K3.11, K7, §28.2 (*The compiler-inserted free*), §28.3 (State match on reassignment; Adoption; Producers `??`/if rows), §28.6, §28.7, §20, §19.2, §22.4; #5768 (closed, ruling reading 1), #5810 (impl tracker), proposal 0162 (item 8: the overwrite reclaims)
cells.note: Decided: owned ⊓ owned carries one obligation; owned ⊓ borrowed is rejected; a conditional kill of any row joins to maybe-consumed with per-path scope-end auto-drop; adoption is per path; a marked arm `move x` consumes on its selected path; null and throw arms absorb. The v0.333 opening (reassigning a maybe-consumed local) is closed by the #5768 ruling: the store takes an owned RHS, disposes the displaced value on the paths that still own it, and leaves the binding owned. New conflict, at the seam of that ruling and proposal 0162: §28.3 says an explicitly-disposed LHS 'displaces nothing' and that a maybe-consumed store disposes 'nothing on the others'. Under 0162, though, explicit `Dispose()` no longer reclaims: the block stays live until the holder's release point (§28.2). For a reassigned local that point can only be the overwrite 'for a displaced value'. §28.7's liveness test (non-null and not moved-from) counts an explicitly-disposed value as live, and §28.2 names 'a drop-on-overwrite over an explicitly disposed value' as a call the language issues. Proposal 0162 item 8 meant exactly that ('the overwrite is the holder's release point and reclaims there'). Under §28.3's sentence, no release point is left for the disposed block, and its free obligation (K1.6: tracked even when trivial) leaks on that path. Logical disposal is exactly-once under both readings.

cells.rule: K7.4: "owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = **maybe-consumed** — unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path" | §28.3: "Reassignment is the one operation the unreadable states admit ("unreadable until reassigned"), which is what makes the loop-carried spelling" | §28.3: "A **moved-from** or **explicitly-disposed** LHS is an owned-state LHS holding no live value: it requires an owned RHS and displaces nothing ([§28.7](#sec-reassigning-owned-fields)'s liveness test)." | §28.2: "the overwrite for a displaced value" | §28.2: "a drop-on-overwrite over an explicitly disposed value" | K3.14: "An owned value that reaches its scope's end undischarged and not moved-from is disposed there implicitly" | §29.2: "the "fall-through to the next iteration" edge is checked the same way as the body's end"
cells.cite: K3.14, K7 (back edges), K7.4, K8.2, §21.4, §21.5, §28.2 (*The compiler-inserted free*), §28.3 (Move semantics: loop accumulator; State match on reassignment), §28.7, §29.2, §28.14 v1 bound 2(a); #5768 (closed), #5810
cells.note: Decided: a `move` inside a loop of a binding declared outside joins maybe-consumed at the back edge and may not flow into the next iteration's use. A body-local owned binding is auto-dropped at each iteration's end and on every jump out of the body. An owning iteration variable is discharged on every body-exit edge. The #5768 ruling makes the loop-carried spelling (`… Take(move r); … r := new Res(); end;`) the stated idiom, so the v0.333 opening is closed for moves. The R1×C7 conflict (L3-R1) recurs per iteration when the carried binding is explicitly disposed instead of moved. `r.Dispose(); r := new Res();` at the body's end 'displaces nothing' under §28.3, so each iteration's disposed block has no release point. Under §28.2/§28.7 each block is reclaimed at the overwrite.

cells.rule: A5: "`using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out" | §28.10: "`using var y := move x;` transfers a named owned local or `owned` parameter into a scope-bound binding: `y` takes over the disposal obligation and `x` is left moved-from" | §30.5: "not a `using var` binding: a `using var` cannot be moved out of ([§28.3](#sec-local-variables-ownership-and-borrows)), so a read of it is a borrow" | §31.1: "a *borrowed* class reference is not a valid operand" | §30.5: "the chained-slot arrangement **defers its disposal** from the frame's scope end to the outer task's teardown"
cells.cite: A5, A12, K3.4, §28.3 (Move semantics), §28.10 (adopting a named owned binding; anonymous binding; compiler-introduced slot), §29.2, §30.5, §31.1
cells.note: Unchanged at v0.334. Into R2: `using var y := move x;` (and `using var _ := move x;`, `out using var`, an owned arm-meet) adopts, and the binding is disposed at its block's end on every exit edge. Out of R2: every transfer is rejected (A5). A Pattern B await or `throw` of a `using var` reads it as a borrow (route cell). A12's Pattern A chaining defers the timing; it is not a move. cells.rule: K9.2: "**the restoration rule**: every control-flow path from a `move` of a field or slot to the enclosing method's exit — normal, `throw`, `yield break`, a suspension's abandonment edge (`yield return`, [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)), and every exception edge raised by an intervening throwable expression — must reassign the slot" | §28.8.1: "**The window is straight-line.** Between a `move` of a field or slot and the store that restores it, no expression evaluated on any path is throwable under the inventory below" | §28.8.1: "A restoration placed in a `finally` or in a `catch` arm does not cover a throwable expression in the protected block" | §28.8.1: "In checked disposal mode a read of it through any spelling other than this body's tracked one — an alias of the holder, code run inside the window (a constructor body, a destructor, a callee where the window admits calls) — faults as `DisposedAccessException`" | §28.8.1: "a store into it other than the restoring store faults the same way **before** storing" | §28.8.1: "no store other than the restoration can give the location a value inside the window, so the restoration displaces nothing and stays non-throwable" | §28.8.1: "The restoring store itself is into a moved-from location, so it is non-throwable" | K9: "A field's obligation belongs to the object: it is discharged by the destructor cascade (owned fields, reverse declaration order) or by drop-on-overwrite, never by any scope's end"

A store other than the restoration faults before storing. The restoring store therefore displaces nothing, and the taken object is disposed once, by the taker. Hunted and closed: `Replace()` under a restoring `finally` (rejected at the call); `new Probe(this)` whose constructor stores into the vacated field (checked fault before the store, K4.1); two parameters aliasing one object, `move a._f` then `move b._f` (the second spelling is untracked, so it faults); `b._f := new Res()` in the window (a possibly-live drop is throwable, so rejected). Under every reading the vacated state keeps the obligation exactly-once and backstops the hole.

An arm that reads a field is a borrow arm, and an arm `move _f` is a fresh-producer arm whose restoration is owed on its selected path.

(owned) _storage[slot] := null; // restore moved-from slot item!.Dispose(); // slot was non-null // (slot < _count guarantees it)" | §27.5: "Modifications to a captured variable inside the lambda are visible outside, and vice versa."

cells.note: Decided: ingress takes `owned`, and an indexer-set drops the displaced element. `Pop*`/`Drain` hand ownership out. The v0.333 'for any `j`' conflict (RC-B) is closed by 0163: the index must be a constant or a local not reassigned before the restoring store, tracked per slot, and a store at another index restores nothing. RC-A is closed by the straight-line window and the vacated state. A slot of a `static owned readonly OwningArray<T>` is moved under a straight-line window, so no call runs. Open, two faces. (1) Conflict: §28.11 names `coll.Clear()` a restoration, but stdlib §4.5's Clear, which 'the standard library provides … directly', does `move _storage[slot]` on every slot below `_count` and asserts the result non-null. On the vacated slot that read faults in checked mode (§28.8.1: a callee's read through another spelling). Unchecked, `item!` raises `NullReferenceException`. The spec-sanctioned restoration therefore raises mid-pass. It stays exactly-once (later cascades skip the vacated slot), but the verdict differs. (2) Ambiguity, only in the window that admits calls (a heap collection held by an owned local): 'a local the body does not reassign' does not say whether a mutably captured index local, or one passed as `ref` in the window, qualifies. §7.4's *stable local* excludes both. If a closure the window invokes changes `k`, the 'restoring' store `pool[k] := t` lands on a live slot. §28.11 says that store does not dispose the previous value, so that element leaks. (The OwningArray reference setter would drop it at run time, which the spec's sentence contradicts.)

In an owned-consuming position the selected value moves (marker-free, the marker rejected) and the binding joins per-path consumed. In a borrowing position every branch is a borrow. The reassignment half (RC-E) is closed by #5768: a maybe-consumed move-only local takes a whole-value store that disposes per path. Statement joins follow K7. A later read of the field is K4.1-backstopped (no static diagnostic). cells.rule: §31.1: "the runtime's dispose-after-arm sets the disposed flag, so a borrow surviving the handler faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode" | §31.1: "Inside a catch arm, the bound exception variable (`var ex: Exception` in the arm pattern) is a **borrow** of the in-flight exception" | K3.5: "at the await, on all outgoing edges including fault and cancel" | §30.5: "any await of an already-disposed task raises `InvalidOperationException`" | §30.9: "The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, at the later of the task's disposal and its settlement**" | §30.5: "The task's own block stays live until that terminal state — its reclamation at the holder's release point is deferred there, never awaited or blocked on" | §28.6: "`Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error."

A task-owned fault is now disposed once 'at the later of the task's disposal and its settlement', and a retained operand task's fault stays with that task (proposal 0168); an explicit kill of an unsettled task attaches the continuation and keeps the task's block live to its terminal state. cells.rule: K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation" | §28.3: "a closure cannot consume, reassign, or dispose a captured owned binding" | §8.6: "Move-only value types — owning inline arrays (`[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`) and owning-classified choices ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) — cannot be boxed."

cells.note: Runtime-managed values carry no classification or obligation, so an explicit `Dispose()` on one is the no-op and no use-after question arises. Hunted for an exemption leaking into an obligation path: a closure cannot dispose (or consume) a captured owned binding; a closure over a borrow of an owned local that is later explicitly disposed reaches the object only through member accesses, which K4.1 flags; move-only values cannot be boxed, so no box hides an owned slot from the kill.

cells.rule: §30.14: "the origin domain loses access **statically at the binding level** — the consumed binding is left moved-from, and the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) rejects the transfer while any local borrow of that binding is live" | §30.14: "class-typed arguments are `owned` and are moved through the spawn into the entry's parameter." | K4.3: "**Recorded trust, or nothing.** Where an admission's temporal guarantee can neither be statically compared (K2.3) nor flag-backstopped — the domain clause ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s field-store bullet, clause 4): a borrowed-from object transferred to, or made reachable from, another domain stays alive, so no flag is ever set" | §28.3 cl.4: "A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below" | §30.1: "every borrow source reaching an async call must outlive the settlement of the returned task" | §30.1: "the borrowed object must not be transferred to another domain"
cells.note: An owned binding crosses only as an `owned` spawn argument or channel `Send` (K3.3, frozen): the origin binding is moved-from, the receiving domain's `owned` parameter / Receive result discharges it, and a raise from the consuming call leaves it with the callee (§28.8.1). Indirect pre-transfer aliases (field-, collection-, comparer-held, pending-frame) are the K4.3-recorded domain clause, explicitly not flag-backstopped; the trust-admission report names them. Hunted: transfer after a dominating Dispose() (warned; the moved object's flag crosses with it under the spawn/channel happens-before edges), a live closure or frame over the binding (frozen), a pending task over it (§30.1 settlement clause). v0.334 hunt: an unawaited direct `c.DisposeAsync()` followed by `Send(move c)` (warned) puts the object in another domain while its DisposeAsync frame still runs on `this` — the §30.1 settlement clause's recorded domain extension (the frame's receiver 'must not be transferred to another domain' before settlement), so the window's in-domain memory-safety claim is not relied on.

cells.rule: A5: "`using var` is a scope pin: non-reassignable, never movable out" | §30.14: "the origin domain loses access **statically at the binding level** — the consumed binding is left moved-from, and the consume-site freeze ([§28.3](#sec-consume-site-freeze)) rejects the transfer while any local borrow of that binding is live" | §30.14: "class-typed arguments are `owned` and are moved through the spawn into the entry's parameter."
cells.note: A `using var` (and every compiler-introduced slot of its kind) is never movable out, and a class value crosses a domain only as an owned transfer, so the holder itself cannot reach another domain; its borrow-pin form owns nothing and a borrow is never sendable. What a scoped binding sends (`sender.Send(BuildReport(1))`, a `Clone()` of a pinned handle) is a fresh value, R3/C13.

cells.rule: §30.14: "class-typed arguments are `owned` and are moved through the spawn into the entry's parameter." | §30.15: "A send that **faults** disposes its class-typed item before the exception surfaces" | §30.15: "Disposing the `Channel<T>` itself closes it immediately and disposes every undelivered class-typed item in reverse insertion order"
cells.cite: K3.3, K8, §28.3 (Unbound owned temporaries), §28.8.1, §30.14, §30.15, stdlib §6.8, §6.9
cells.note: A fresh temporary passed to an `owned` spawn argument or `Send` transfers at call entry and is discharged on the receiving side; a faulting send disposes the item before the exception surfaces, a channel disposes undelivered items in reverse insertion order, and a temporary whose consuming call is never entered is disposed by the caller's unwind. Plain spawn rows admit no class type, so no temporary crosses as a borrow.

cells.rule: §30.14 rule 2: "an owning-inline-array field (`[N owned]C` / `[N owned]C?`) whose element class is a sendable class type" | §28.3 cl.4: "A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below" | K4.3: "**Recorded trust, or nothing.** Where an admission's temporal guarantee can neither be statically compared (K2.3) nor flag-backstopped — the domain clause ([§28.3](#sec-borrow-lifetime-rules)'s field-store bullet, clause 4): a borrowed-from object transferred to, or made reachable from, another domain stays alive, so no flag is ever set" | §30.1: "the borrowed object must not be transferred to another domain" | §28.2: "Where a direct `DisposeAsync()`'s task has not reached its terminal state at the holder's release point, reclamation is deferred to that terminal state: the release point neither awaits nor blocks"
cells.cite: K4.3, K5.6, K9.2, §28.3 (field-store cl.4), §28.4, §30.14 (transfer-closed rule 2), #5725
cells.note: An owned field crosses only inside its holder's owned transfer (transfer-closed rule 2 requires every owned field sendable), so its obligation moves with the tree and the receiving domain's teardown cascades over it; `move box.f` into a spawn argument or `Send` is an ordinary K9.2 take plus transfer. A borrow of the field's current value left in the origin domain is the recorded domain clause (not flag-backstopped), named by the trust-admission report. v0.334 hunt: an explicitly disposed or in-flight-DisposeAsync field riding its holder's transfer — the receiving domain's cascade issues the no-op Dispose() and the single free (deferred to the terminal state for an in-flight call); the in-flight frame's `this` is held under the §30.1 settlement clause.

cells.rule: §30.14: "an owning collection iff its element type is a sendable class type" | §30.14: "Moved-in items that were never processed are disposed by the runtime" | §30.15: "Disposing the `Channel<T>` itself closes it immediately and disposes every undelivered class-typed item in reverse insertion order"
cells.cite: §28.11, §30.14 (sendable statements; data-parallel combinators), §30.15, stdlib §4.5–§4.12, §6.9, §6.12
cells.note: Sub-shapes: an owning collection crosses as one owned transfer iff its element type is sendable (its slots move with it, once); a borrowing collection of class elements is not sendable (rejected); `Parallel.*` over `owned items` moves the elements to workers and the runtime disposes unprocessed ones; a channel's buffered items are slots of the channel, disposed once on its disposal. A slot taken by `move coll[i]` into a spawn is the R4 domain-clause shape.

cells.rule: §30.14: "**Value types** are sendable iff they are not borrow-bearing ([§9.7](#sec-records-and-disposal)), not move-only ([§15.3](#sec-move-only-value-types)), and **every component type is sendable**." | §30.14 rule 2: "an owning-inline-array field (`[N owned]C` / `[N owned]C?`) whose element class is a sendable class type" | §8.6: "Move-only value types — owning inline arrays (`[N owned]T` and `[N owned]T?`) and owning-classified choices ([§35.4](#sec-choice-classification)) — cannot be boxed."
cells.cite: §8.6, §15.3, §30.14 (value-type rule; transfer-closed rule 2), §35.12
cells.note: A move-only value is never sendable by itself (value-type rule) and cannot be boxed past the check, so a spawn argument, result or channel element of that type is rejected. As an owning-inline-array or owning-choice field of a sendable class it rides its holder's owned transfer and is disposed once by the receiving domain's cascade.

cells.rule: §30.14: "An exception that propagates out of the entry does not cross the boundary as an object" | §30.14: "The entry's task object never crosses the boundary: it lives and dies in the spawned domain" | §30.9: "The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, at the later of the task's disposal and its settlement**" | §30.15: "A send that **faults** disposes its class-typed item before the exception surfaces"
cells.note: No exception and no task object crosses: an entry's escaping exception is owned by the entry task in the spawned domain and disposed with it, while the join raises a fresh DomainFaultedException carrying copied strings; the join handle is an ordinary task of the spawning domain (Pattern B result transfer for `OwningTask<R>`). A pending `Receive` disposed before handoff gives the item back, and a faulting send disposes its item.

cells.rule: §30.14: "The entry's task object never crosses the boundary: it lives and dies in the spawned domain" | §30.1: "every borrow source reaching an async call must outlive the settlement of the returned task" | §28.3 cl.4: "A field-stored borrow of an object later moved across a domain boundary — directly, or through a different binding such as `move box.f` into a spawn argument or channel send — is *not* rejected by the consume-site freeze below" | K6.4: "A **task's** are not traced by K5: their outlives-obligation is the K4.3-recorded settlement clause"
cells.cite: K6, K6.4, K4.3, §28.3 (field-store cl.5), §30.1, §30.14 (Domain completion), stdlib §6.8
cells.note: Frames are interface- or Task-typed and never sendable, so no frame crosses; an `async` entry's task lives and dies in the spawned domain, and pending tasks left there continue under FireAndForget handling. A borrow a pending frame holds of an object later transferred to another domain is the §30.1 settlement clause's recorded domain extension (K4.3), not flag-backstopped.

cells.rule: §28.6: "a `static owned` field read (a borrow of [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source, which only [§22.13](#sec-disposal-of-static-owned-fields)'s exit pass disposes — [K9.4](#sec-kernel-k9))" | K9.4: "static owned storage — a `static owned` field, and the slots of a `static readonly` owning inline array ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) note (h)) — admits no `move`, no slot store and no explicit disposal" | K4.3: "No clause covers a **static-held** borrow, and none is needed" | K4.3: "across domains the flag is no backstop, so the always-live holder admits only what lives as long as it does." | §22.12 rule 4: "the referenced instance is reachable from every domain, and confining its use to one domain — or ensuring its own internal synchronization — is the programmer's obligation" | §22.13: "No other Bezel code runs concurrently during the shutdown sequence"
cells.cite: K2, K4.3, K9.4, §22.12 rule 4, §22.13 (Disposal of static owned fields; shutdown thread), §28.3 (Static stores), §28.6, §30.12; #5760 (closed); #5807 (impl)
cells.note: Closed by proposal 0162 item 4: no code may dispose a `static owned` field (or a `static readonly` owning-inline-array slot) before exit, so the always-live classification K2, the Static-stores bullet and K4.3 rely on now holds; the exit pass disposes it once, on the shutdown thread, with no other Bezel code running. Rule 4's backstop clause is struck. What remains cross-domain is a kill *inside* the static's referent (an owned field's early release, an element removal), which is rule 4's warned confinement obligation, and for a lock reached that way §30.12's checked-mode detection (route). Hunted: a warning-suppression-set static (`Mutex`, `CancellationTokenSource`) disposed early (rejected), a domain still live at exit (§33.3: abandoned, not resumed).

cells.rule: §30.14: "**`string`** and **`Type`** are sendable; each crosses as a shared reference, which is safe because both are immutable" | §30.14: "**Function-typed values are never sendable**: their captures are borrows of the origin domain's scopes" | K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation"
cells.cite: K1.6, §28.9, §30.14 (string/Type bullet; function types; boxed values)
cells.note: `string` and `Type` cross as shared immutable references, a boxed value only if its type is sendable, and a function value never; none carries an obligation, so no cross-domain disposal question arises. Hunted: a function value smuggling captured owned bindings across (never sendable, and spawn entries are capture-free).

cells.rule: §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field or owning-collection slot read by code of the owning object's declaring type" | K3.9: "logical disposal at the end of the discard statement ([§17.13](#sec-the-discard-_)) or at the call (for `DisposeAsync()`, completing at the returned task's terminal state, [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)); reclamation at the holder's release point" | §28.12: "A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has **begun** is a no-op" | §28.12: "the per-instance flag records the beginning of logical disposal — at the `Dispose()` call, at the direct `DisposeAsync()` call, or at `await using`'s scope exit, before the body's first statement — and the `DisposeAsync()` no-op returns a completed task" | §28.12: "An instance is **logically disposed** — the state [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s checked-mode test faults on — once its logical disposal has completed" | §28.12: "A member access through any other alias while a direct `DisposeAsync()` is in flight is [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s program error, faulting in checked mode from the task's terminal state on; inside the window it reaches an instance whose block and owned fields are intact" | §28.2: "Where a direct `DisposeAsync()`'s task has not reached its terminal state at the holder's release point, reclamation is deferred to that terminal state: the release point neither awaits nor blocks" | §28.12: "on the same owned binding the second explicit call, whichever of the two it is, is [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s use-after-dispose warning"
cells.cite: K3.9, K4.2, K5.3, §28.2 (compiler-inserted free), §28.6, §28.12 (steps 1–2; second-call paragraph), §30.1; #5758 (closed), #5830 (impl), #5660 (impl)
cells.note: Closed by proposal 0162 (option H′): the flag records the *beginning* of logical disposal, so a second Dispose() or DisposeAsync() inside a direct DisposeAsync()'s window is a no-op (a completed task for DisposeAsync) and draws §28.2's warning on the same binding; the cascade and chain run once at the terminal state, and the block is released at the later of the holder's release point and that state, never blocking. An alias's access inside the window is §28.2's program error on an intact block, faulting in checked mode from the terminal state on. Implicit discharge (auto-drop, unwind) is synchronous. Hunted: second call in-window (no-op), `move c` in-window to a synchronous owner (its free is deferred), `await using var d := move c;` in-window (scope exit's DisposeAsync is a no-op), a DisposeAsync that faults (cascade then propagation), transfer to another domain in-window (§30.1 settlement clause, R1/C13), Main ending in-window (§33.3: pending effects lost, recorded).

cells.rule: §28.12: "**The `DisposeAsync` awaited is the run-time object's.**" | §28.12: "Over an owned right-hand side with no `DisposeAsync` to await — a value-type, runtime-managed or move-only right-hand side, or an object whose class does not implement `IAsyncDisposable` — scope exit takes the synchronous disposal (or the no-op) and likewise awaits nothing." | §30.7: "On **early abandonment** — the consumer disposes a suspended iterator — [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous disposal pass takes [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s synchronous-fallback path for every `await using var` active at the suspension point" | §28.6: "the scope-end machinery of a `using var` or `await using var` whose `DisposeAsync()` was called directly skips it like any explicitly-disposed binding" | §28.12: "A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has **begun** is a no-op" | §28.12: "the per-instance flag records the beginning of logical disposal — at the `Dispose()` call, at the direct `DisposeAsync()` call, or at `await using`'s scope exit, before the body's first statement — and the `DisposeAsync()` no-op returns a completed task" | §28.12: "The `Dispose()` the runtime issues to complete an `await using` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` (step 2's cascade and chain) is that disposal's own step, not a second call."
cells.cite: A5, §28.6, §28.10, §28.12 (await using; run-time object; sync fallback), §29.7, §30.7; #5653, #5654 (impl); #5758 (closed)
cells.note: `await using var` is decided on every edge it owns: it awaits the run-time object's DisposeAsync on the normal and exception edges, disposes synchronously when there is nothing to await, takes the synchronous fallback on early iterator abandonment (§30.7 rejects fallback-less types across a yield), and a borrow-pin awaits nothing. The flag is set at scope exit before the body's first statement, and the runtime's completing Dispose() is that disposal's own step, not a second call. The direct-call face that kept it open is closed with R1/C14: a direct DisposeAsync() on the binding makes scope exit skip it, and a second call in-window is the no-op. Hunted: an alias access while `await using`'s own DisposeAsync is suspended (not logically disposed until completion, block intact; faults from completion on).

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §28.3: "A temporary that is instead bound (to a `var`/`using var`), `move`d, returned, or transferred into an owning location is governed by the corresponding transfer or discharge rule and is **not** disposed under this rule (it would otherwise be disposed twice)." | §28.12: "the block is released then or at the holder's release point, whichever comes later — abandonment delays reclamation, it never skips it" | §28.3: "an explicit `Dispose()` or direct `DisposeAsync()` on it is [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)'s consume, not a borrowing use, after which the boundary reclaims only ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal))." | §28.3: "whose sources are the call's receiver and the sources its plain arguments contribute"
cells.cite: K8.1, K8.4, §28.3 (Unbound owned temporaries; Deferred-activation callees), §28.12 (Implicit discharge is synchronous; abandoned DisposeAsync task), §17.13, A6
cells.note: A temporary's boundary disposal is implicit and synchronous (the no-destructor warning covers the class side). `Make().DisposeAsync()` is K3.9's consume, after which the boundary reclaims only, and the release is deferred to the task's terminal state; the temporary is the frame's receiver source, so binding or storing the returned task past the full expression is rejected by the deferred-activation rule, and awaiting it in place is once. An abandoned DisposeAsync task still runs to its terminal state; 'abandonment delays reclamation, it never skips it'.

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §28.6: "requires a receiver the disposer **owns** (derives: [K3.9](#sec-kernel-k3)): an owned local or `owned` parameter, a `using var`, an unbound owned temporary ([§28.3](#sec-unbound-owned-temporaries)), a `move` result, or an `owned` field or owning-collection slot read by code of the owning object's declaring type" | §28.6: "The call is an **early release point**, not a discharge of the slot's obligation: the slot keeps its reference and its [K9](#sec-kernel-k9) obligation, and the containing object's teardown still runs the cascade over it ([§28.4](#sec-the-destructor) step 2), where the second call is [§28.2](#sec-the-idisposable-contract)'s no-op" | §28.12: "A second call to `Dispose()` or `DisposeAsync()` after either has **begun** is a no-op" | §28.2: "so the `Dispose()` the language itself issues there — the cascade over an explicitly disposed field, a drop-on-overwrite over an explicitly disposed value, the exit pass — reads a live flag in both modes" | §28.2: "Where a direct `DisposeAsync()`'s task has not reached its terminal state at the holder's release point, reclamation is deferred to that terminal state: the release point neither awaits nor blocks" | §28.12: "owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order and the base class's reclamation chains, once, immediately after logical disposal has completed, whichever path ran"
cells.cite: §28.2 (compiler-inserted free), §28.4, §28.6 (early release), §28.12 (steps 1–2; second call; Implicit discharge is synchronous; fallback warning), §30.1; #5758, #5759 (closed)
cells.note: The cascade over an `owned` field is implicit and synchronous (async-only cleanup skipped, warned at the class). The declaring type's direct `_f.DisposeAsync()` is an early release: awaited, the later cascade call is the no-op on a live block (R4/C9); unawaited, the owner's teardown issues Dispose() inside the window, which is a no-op because the flag records the beginning, and the field's block is released at the later of the teardown and the terminal state, never blocking. The field's own cascade and chain run once at that terminal state. Hunted: teardown then a field-held back-reference read by the in-flight DisposeAsync body (the parent is logically disposed: K4.1 field-held backstop), reassigning `_f` in-window (drop-on-overwrite no-op; release deferred).

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §28.6: "an element borrow of an **owning** collection (`pool[i].Dispose()` — use `Remove`/`RemoveAt`, the indexer-set, or `move coll[i]`, whose forms keep the slot state coherent" | §28.6: "`Dispose()` or a direct `DisposeAsync()` call through a **borrow** is a compile error."
cells.cite: §28.6, §28.11, §28.12 (Implicit discharge is synchronous)
cells.note: Container cascades, `Remove`/`Clear` and the indexer-set's displacement are implicit and synchronous. An element's own `DisposeAsync()` through an element borrow is the borrow-receiver error. Asynchronous per-element cleanup is spelled by taking the element out (`Drain()`, `Pop*`, `move coll[i]`) into an owned binding and using `await using` on it, which is R1/R2.

cells.rule: §28.12: "Over an owned right-hand side with no `DisposeAsync` to await — a value-type, runtime-managed or move-only right-hand side, or an object whose class does not implement `IAsyncDisposable` — scope exit takes the synchronous disposal (or the no-op) and likewise awaits nothing." | §35.9: "`Dispose` stays off the surface everywhere: choices do not implement `IDisposable`" | §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown"
cells.note: Move-only values have no `DisposeAsync`, so `await using var` over one awaits nothing and disposes slots or payloads synchronously. An `IAsyncDisposable` payload or slot object is disposed by its holder's implicit, synchronous pass.

cells.rule: §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown" | §30.9: "The exception is disposed **exactly once, by the task that owns it, at the later of the task's disposal and its settlement**" | §31.1: "the runtime's dispose-after-arm sets the disposed flag, so a borrow surviving the handler faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException` in checked disposal mode"
cells.note: Task teardown's disposal of an unconsumed result, a task's disposal of its owned fault exception, and the runtime's dispose-after-arm all run from synchronous, implicit positions and take the synchronous path. A Pattern B result is handed to the awaiter, which may `await using` it (R2). Note: the dispose-after-arm path is not in §28.12's enumerated list, but nothing at those positions can await.

cells.rule: §30.7: "On **early abandonment** — the consumer disposes a suspended iterator — [§29.7](#sec-disposal-of-partially-consumed-iterators)'s synchronous disposal pass takes [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal)'s synchronous-fallback path for every `await using var` active at the suspension point" | §30.7: "therefore **may not be live across a `yield return`** in an async iterator" | §29.1: "a `Dispose()`/`DisposeAsync()` after an advance whose value was never taken **disposes the pending value**" | §28.12: "**Implicit discharge is synchronous.** The implicit disposal paths — auto-drop of a plain-`var` owned local or undischarged `owned` parameter at scope end, the exception-path cleanup, drop-on-overwrite, container cascades, and frame teardown"
cells.cite: K6, §28.12, §29.7, §29.8, §30.1, §30.7 (await for; await in finally; yield-liveness rule), §29.1; #5654 (impl), #5657
cells.note: `await for` acquires the async enumerator under `await using`. Early abandonment runs §29.7's synchronous pass with the per-binding synchronous fallback, `await` in a source-written `finally` of an async iterator is rejected, and fallback-less `await using` bindings may not be live across a yield. An untaken pending value is disposed by `DisposeAsync()` as by `Dispose()`. Frame teardown of `owned` parameters is implicit and synchronous. Hunted: disposing an async enumerator while a `MoveNextAsync` task is pending violates the §30.1 settlement clause on the receiver, and the resumption's field access faults in checked mode (L5's columns).

cells.rule: §22.13: "Static `owned` fields are disposed at program exit, after `Main` completes" | §22.13: "the destructors the pass invokes" | §22.13: "No other Bezel code runs concurrently during the shutdown sequence" | §28.6: "a `static owned` field read (a borrow of [K2](#sec-kernel-k2)'s always-live source, which only [§22.13](#sec-disposal-of-static-owned-fields)'s exit pass disposes — [K9.4](#sec-kernel-k9))" | K9.4: "static owned storage — a `static owned` field, and the slots of a `static readonly` owning inline array ([§22.12](#sec-static-members) note (h)) — admits no `move`, no slot store and no explicit disposal" | §28.12: "Asynchronous cleanup runs only where the program wrote `await using`" | §33.3: "their owned state is reclaimed by the process exit, not by disposal, and their pending effects are lost"
cells.cite: K9.4, §22.13 (Disposal of static owned fields; shutdown thread), §28.6, §28.12 (Implicit discharge is synchronous), §33.3; #5758, #5760 (closed)
cells.note: Closed by proposal 0162 item 4: a direct DisposeAsync() through a `static owned` field is the borrow-receiver error (K9.4), so no in-flight window can open on always-live storage. The exit pass is the one discharger: it runs on the shutdown thread, alone, and asynchronous cleanup runs only where the program wrote `await using` or awaited a direct call, so the pass takes the synchronous path (the no-destructor warning covers an async-only class). Hunted: an in-flight DisposeAsync on a field of a static's referent when Main ends — its continuation never resumes (§33.3's recorded live-domain posture: reclaimed by process exit, pending effects lost); the exit pass's cascade over that field is the no-op.

cells.rule: §28.12: "Over an owned right-hand side with no `DisposeAsync` to await — a value-type, runtime-managed or move-only right-hand side, or an object whose class does not implement `IAsyncDisposable` — scope exit takes the synchronous disposal (or the no-op) and likewise awaits nothing." | K1.6: "Values of runtime-managed type (`string`, `Type`, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation"
cells.note: `await using var` over a runtime-managed value takes the no-op and awaits nothing, and no runtime-managed type carries an obligation for an async path to discharge.

cells.note: Decided legs: awaiting an owning-collection slot of `Task<T>` (Pattern A borrow) or `OwningTask<T>` (disposed in place, later awaits raise `InvalidOperationException`); the drain-await idiom; a `move coll[i]` window across an `await` on a field-held collection is now rejected (straight-line, proposal 0163). New open leg: the collection window over a heap collection held by an owned local of the body carries no straight-line obligation, so a callee or a concurrent continuation holding a borrow of the collection can run during it. A read or store of the vacated slot faults (checked), but a structural modification (`Insert`, `RemoveAt` of another index, `Reverse`) relocates the vacated slot while the analysis tracks it 'per slot, at that index'. Reading A: relocating the slot is a read of it through another spelling, so it faults in checked mode (and an `Add` that reallocates would fault too). Reading B: the vacated state moves with the slot; the restoring store at the tracked index, emitted without the test and displacing nothing, overwrites a live element, which leaks in both modes, and the moved slot is skipped by the cascade. The synchronous twin (a plain callee `Grow` in the window) is R5/C5's, so the C10 cell is the suspension-widened face.

New open leg: a **Pattern B borrowed operand** (an owned field, an owning slot, static storage, a `using var`) whose fault escapes. §30.5 has the await dispose such an operand in place, and §30.9 times that disposal as the await's terminal act, which for an escaping fault falls at the capture; the instance is disposed with its owning task 'at the later of the task's disposal and its settlement', which is then. §30.9's retention says the faulted task carries the instance as a borrow, that the borrowed operand must outlive every await of the faulted task, and that every awaiter re-raises 'the same live instance'. The language's own await breaks that obligation every time, and §28.12's cascade reclaims the instance at that logical disposal, so the K4.3 flag test reads a released block. routes.route: return slot: the disposal moment when the raising return-edge cleanup belongs to a scope enclosing the `return` statement's
routes.rule: §28.3: "established on the cleanup stack at the `return` statement, after the operand's evaluation and before the scope's cleanups run" | §28.3: "the call completes by the exception unless a handler in the callee catches it — and the slot's value is disposed by the unwind as an owned local established at that point would be, when the exception leaves the `return` statement's scope" | §28.10: "a cleanup that raises leaves the value to the callee's unwind"
routes.note: The holder is decided; the moment is not. The slot's value is disposed 'when the exception leaves the `return` statement's scope', but the slot must outlive every return-edge cleanup, including those of enclosing scopes (an outer `using var`, an enclosing `try`'s `finally`), whose raise happens after the `return` statement's scope was already left on the normal edge. Reading A: the slot is the newest pending entry, disposed first in that unwind (before any further `finally` and before a callee handler's arm). Reading B: the 'scope' is the method body the return exits, so the value is disposed only as the exception leaves the method, after every remaining cleanup, and never if a callee handler catches it (a leak). The difference is observable as destructor order and, under B, a leak.

routes.route: a scope-end disposal (inner block's owned local or `using var`, or a K8 boundary) that raises inside a straight-line restoration window

Reading 1 (#5796's recommendation): the edge is admitted and the method exits with the field vacated for good; its value belongs to the taker, disposed in the unwind, the cascade disposes nothing through the location, and later reads fault in checked mode (once-backstopped, but 'no hole' is stated only for a fault-left location). routes.route: Environment.Exit called by a destructor (or a lazy static initializer) that the program-exit pass runs
routes.rule: §33.3: "**`Environment.Exit(code)`:** callable from any domain; it initiates the same shutdown sequence (no further continuations anywhere, static `owned` disposal on the dedicated shutdown thread, then process exit with `code`). It never returns." | §22.13: "The runtime guarantees disposal occurs on a single, dedicated **shutdown thread**, which — like the startup thread — runs **outside any domain**" | §33.3: "Every determination above fixes the exit code **before** [§22.13](#sec-static-initialization-order)'s shutdown pass begins" | §33.3: "and no event inside the pass changes it"
routes.cite: §33.3, §22.13 (shutdown thread; drain; exit-time throws), §28.3 (abandoned frames), stdlib §2.4; #5779 ruling
routes.note: The #5779 ruling decides `Environment.Exit` from a live frame; it does not say what the call does from the exit pass itself, whose destructors and lazily triggered static initializers run on a shutdown thread 'outside any domain' (the call is stated 'callable from any domain'). Readings: (A) it re-initiates the sequence, re-entering a pass that is mid-way, so the pass's statics and the `code` change; (B) it terminates at once, the pass's frame abandoned like any live frame, so every static the pass had not reached yet is reclaimed but never disposed, against §22.13's graceful-shutdown guarantee; (C) it is a no-op or an error there. The exit code is also unsettled: 'no event inside the pass changes it' versus the call's own `code`.

A `Get()` borrow is bounded by its handle. A field-held borrow of a handle later moved away is the recorded domain clause.

For a trivial-dispose field the explicit call sets the flag and runs no user code.

routes.route: the chained base.DisposeAsync() in a DisposeAsync override (zero, one or two calls)
routes.rule: §28.6: "in the body of a `DisposeAsync` override itself, not in a lambda nested in it, `base.DisposeAsync()` is [§28.12](#sec-asynchronous-disposal) step 2's chain, not a disposal of `this`, and is admitted" | §28.12: "an override that does not chain forgoes that level's asynchronous cleanup, and its destructor body is skipped all the same" | §28.12: "an override's chained `base.DisposeAsync()` is not such a call but a step of the logical disposal already under way, and triggers no reclamation of its own" | §28.12: "owned fields are disposed in reverse declaration order and the base class's reclamation chains, once, immediately after logical disposal has completed, whichever path ran" | §28.12: "An instance is **logically disposed** — the state [§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)'s checked-mode test faults on — once its logical disposal has completed"
routes.note: A `DisposeAsync` override's `base.DisposeAsync()` is a step of the logical disposal already under way and triggers no reclamation; its accesses are the disposal's own and run on a live instance. Not chaining forgoes the base level's async cleanup by statement; chaining twice re-runs user code only, since the owned-field cascade and chain run once, immediately after logical disposal completes. No language-managed obligation is doubled or leaked.

routes.route: A15 self-returning enumerator: a loop's enumerator disposal logically disposes a borrowed receiver its owner still holds
routes.rule: A15: "the disposal of a self-returned frame runs `Dispose()` without reclaiming" | §29.1: "The disposal of a self-returned frame therefore **runs the object's `Dispose()` and does not reclaim it**" | §29.1: "so the object is reclaimed exactly once however many times its enumerator face is taken and disposed — including when the receiver is a borrow the caller does not own" | K4.1: "in checked disposal mode ([§28.2](#sec-checked-disposal)) any later use through any alias faults deterministically as `DisposedAccessException`"
routes.note: Unchanged at v0.334. A `for` over a borrowed self-returning enumerator logically disposes the owner's object at loop end, reclaim left to the owner (A15); the destructor runs once, and the owner's later use faults under K4.1. Proposal 0162's 'explicit disposal marks, the holder frees' generalizes A15's non-reclaiming disposal, so the block is live when the owner's later use tests the flag.

routes.route: §30.11 completion-source carve: task object owned by the source; late completion and source disposal
routes.rule: §30.11: "**Task-object ownership.** The **source owns the task object** its `Task` property exposes." | §30.11: "For either kind, a **never-awaited** task is disposed exactly once, by the source at source disposal." | §30.11: "A source disposed before completion first faults the task (below) and then disposes it" | §30.11: "If `TrySetResult` returns `false` because the task is already in a terminal state, the implementation disposes `result` before returning."
routes.cite: §30.11 (Task-object ownership; Common semantics; four-condition carve), A10, §30.5, §30.9
routes.note: Unchanged at v0.334. The completion source owns its task; awaits borrow it; a never-awaited task is disposed once with the source; a source disposed before completion faults then disposes the task, which is therefore settled (0168's unsettled-disposal continuation is not engaged); a losing `TrySet*` disposes its argument. No escape found.

routes.route: async enumerator disposed while a `MoveNextAsync()` advance is in flight (frame suspended at an `await`, not at a `yield return`)
routes.rule: §29.7: "When a consumer stops iterating early — `break`, exception, or `using var` ending before exhaustion — the iterator is disposed." | §29.7: "Runs the pending cleanup actions active at the point of suspension" | §29.7: "so nothing resumes and no suspended body runs again" | §30.7: "it acquires an async enumerator with `await using`, calls `MoveNextAsync()` with `await` in a loop." | §30.5: "the `Dispose()` call attaches a **continuation** that runs at the terminal state and disposes there whatever the frame delivers into the task" | §30.5: "The task's own block stays live until that terminal state"
routes.cite: §29.1, §29.7, §30.5 (*Disposing an unsettled or unconsumed task*), §30.7, §28.12, §28.2 (*The compiler-inserted free*), stdlib §4.12, §4.13, #2624 (implementation, completed advance only)
routes.note: New escape. `await for` never disposes the enumerator with an advance in flight, but the manual protocol can: `await using var en := Gen(); using var adv := en.MoveNextAsync();` ends its block while the frame is suspended at an internal `await`. §29.7 is written for a consumer that stops between advances ('the point of suspension', then a completed machine where 'nothing resumes'). It does not say what disposing a frame mid-advance does: whether the pending advance's task is settled (and with what), whether `DisposeAsync()` waits for it, or whether it raises. Read literally, the pass runs at the `await` and completes the machine, the `MoveNextAsync()` task never reaches the terminal state that proposal 0168's continuation and deferred block release wait for (a leak of both), and the awaited operand's later completion resumes into a disposed frame. The synchronous twin needs re-entrancy through a callback, so it is a general C9 question and is not opened here.
